summary: Mission P.I.E.D.R.A. is a bilingual browser game developed by JIIMATZIN for children aged 7–12. During ten training sols at Mars Base One, players allocate limited power, maintain life-support systems and respond to emergencies while managing energy, oxygen and shielding. Three crew specialists offer different routes through an isometric base. NASA mission references and Perseverance audio connect the experience to real exploration, while a NOAA-trained solar forecast introduces uncertainty into decision-making. The companion P.I.E.D.R.A. estimates progress with Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and adapts guidance through teaching rules and Thompson sampling. A separate scientific-content pipeline prepares traceable REMS, DONKI, RadLab and OSDR material for versioned scenarios; its API deployment is distinguished from the public static build. The project aims to help children explain the costs and consequences of their choices. It includes English and Spanish text, keyboard and touch interactions, and a downloadable report of in-game observations and model-based estimates.
details:
Mission P.I.E.D.R.A.: Every Choice Keeps the Base Running

Six power cores. Nine allocation slots. At the command console of Mars Base One, there is more capacity to fill than power to distribute. Life support, energy systems and shielding compete for the same limited supply. The player must decide what receives power now and face what that choice means for the rest of the sol.

This is the starting point of Mission P.I.E.D.R.A., a bilingual browser game for children aged 7 to 12. Across ten training sols, a young astronaut manages energy, oxygen and shielding, maintains equipment and responds to emergencies. The mission answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge through an experience in which scientific ideas become decisions with observable consequences.

The meaning of P.I.E.D.R.A.

The name takes its letters from six actions in Spanish. Each action appears below with its English translation.

  • P. Preparar: revisar la nave, el equipo y el clima antes del despegue.
    Prepare: check the spacecraft, equipment and weather before takeoff.
  • I. Iniciar el viaje: viajar y aterrizar en Marte.
    Initiate the journey: travel to Mars and land there.
  • E. Explorar: recorrer el terreno con el rover.
    Explore: travel across the terrain with the rover.
  • D. Detectar: buscar señales de agua, de vida o de peligros.
    Detect: look for signs of water, life or hazards.
  • R. Recolectar: tomar muestras de rocas y suelo.
    Collect: take rock and soil samples.
  • A. Avisar: analizar los datos y mandar el reporte a la Tierra.
    Report: analyze the data and send the report to Earth.

A small base, a shared responsibility

The mission begins with a choice of crew specialist: Wenceslao, Judith or Atlas. Each follows a different route through the isometric base, giving the same mission a different starting perspective. P.I.E.D.R.A., the robot companion, accompanies the player with instructions, explanations and guidance. A tutorial sol introduces the controls and routines before emergencies enter the campaign.

Each morning brings a new allocation decision. During the day, the player moves between stations to clean solar panels, adapt a CO2-filter connection and care for the greenhouse. An emergency then asks the player to compare alternatives and act with the resources available. At night, the shelter and mission memories create a pause to review what happened before the next sol begins.

The campaign continues through ten sols or ends when a resource reaches zero. Replaying offers a way to revisit the same constraints, choose another specialist and compare strategies. The learning objective runs through this cycle: observe the situation, make a choice, examine its consequences and explain what could change next time.

Explore the mission-cycle diagram.

Real exploration behind the mission

The base is fictional; the evidence behind its scientific context has identifiable origins. Opportunity connects the panel activity with the relationship between dust and solar-energy availability. Apollo 13 provides the engineering reference for adapting a connection that helps remove CO2. Veggie, zinnias and the OSDR/OSD-268 lettuce study connect plant care with research aboard the International Space Station. Wind and dust-devil recordings from Perseverance/SuperCam bring sounds recorded on Mars into the experience.

The scientific-content package extends this context with Curiosity REMS temperature and pressure observations from source sols 10 to 19, a historical DONKI solar-flare catalogue and an ISS radiation sample from RadLab/DosTel1. These sources retain their mission, instrument, dates and units. REMS describes the Martian exterior; RadLab describes an ISS measurement; the lettuce study provides research context for cultivation. They play different educational roles.

That distinction also shapes the game rules. A flare class does not calculate an astronaut’s radiation dose, and an exterior temperature does not directly determine a habitat’s energy consumption. Resource levels, costs, rewards and alert thresholds belong to the educational simulation. The greenhouse’s ISS-inspired microgravity motif is an adaptation rather than a representation of Martian gravity. Keeping evidence and adaptation distinct makes the scientific context traceable without attributing fictional operating parameters to NASA.

Uncertainty becomes part of the player’s reasoning through the solar forecast. A logistic-regression model uses NOAA SWPC Daily Solar Data to estimate whether the following Earth day will contain at least one M- or X-class flare. The browser attempts to refresh the observations and uses a stored, dated copy when the request fails. For days whose outcomes are already recorded, P.I.E.D.R.A. can compare its estimate with what actually happened. The estimate is a project model for exploring uncertainty, not an official NOAA warning or a Mars radiation-dose prediction.

DONKI serves a separate purpose: its recent-event query supplies solar news for the communications antenna. Those records provide context and do not directly trigger game hazards. Together, the forecast and the event catalogue offer two different encounters with evidence: anticipating an uncertain outcome and examining an observed event.

A companion that responds to the player

P.I.E.D.R.A. connects mission events with opportunities to practice. Bayesian Knowledge Tracing updates mastery estimates for four topics: energy, air, shielding and deciding with data. These estimates draw on minigame results, allocation choices and emergency responses. Teaching rules use those observations to select suitable hints, worked examples, explanations and review.

When more than one form of help is appropriate, a Thompson-sampling bandit selects among them and updates from the next observation on the same topic. The combination gives the companion a defined role in the mission: guide the next decision, explain an outcome and revisit a concept that needs practice.

At the end of the mission, a downloadable report brings together recorded actions and estimated progress. Teachers and families can use it to discuss why the player made a choice and what another strategy might accomplish. These indicators are model-based estimates for guidance; educational effectiveness requires a separate evaluation with users.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

The mission connects an interactive game, a scientific content service and statistical models. Each part has a defined technical role:

  • JavaScript, Phaser 4.2.1 and HTML5/CSS: the isometric base, interactive scenes, movement, interface and maintenance activities. JavaScript ES modules, an event bus and shared mission state coordinate the player’s actions and their consequences.
  • Ink and inkjs: narrative progression, dialogue and mission events connect the story with decisions in the base.
  • Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL: the content API and database organize versioned scenarios, reviewed fact cards, source attribution and validated session records.
  • Python and NumPy: scientific data processing and solar forecast training. JSON Schema validates record structures, and SHA-256 fingerprints identify preserved source captures. Quality selection and hourly aggregation retain counts and lineage.
  • Logistic regression, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and Thompson sampling: browser calculations support the solar forecast, estimates of progress and selection of suitable guidance.
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages: the public repository contains the source code, technical documentation and automated backend tests. Cloud hosts the final frontend connected to the project API, while GitHub Pages hosts the static test version.
  • Hardware and access: a computer or touch device with a web browser provides the game interface. The game requires no dedicated sensors, controllers or installation. Backend operation requires its configured service and PostgreSQL database.

Together, these components connect a choice at the console with an updated resource state, a narrative response and feedback from P.I.E.D.R.A. The content adapter links that experience with available scenario data.

The Cloud deployment connects the game to the project API, which serves the published Base Marte Uno scenario. The adapter supports API scenarios and exported JSON fallback. GitHub Pages remains a static test version without the backend connection. Backend tests cover routes, validation, configuration and integration.

Access decisions shape the experience as much as the software does. Three central resources keep the mission focused. English and Spanish text, keyboard, pointer and touch interactions, a minimap, contextual instructions and optional sound offer different ways to follow the mission. Some labels embedded in room artwork remain in Spanish. Broad device compatibility and formal accessibility conformance require their own verification.

Progress records use device and session codes, and the interface does not request player names or email addresses. Server persistence depends on an available backend. Stored NOAA observations and content fallback paths support continuity when external requests fail.

Follow the architecture and data-flow diagrams; Explore the adaptive-guidance flow; Read the learning-model documentation.

From completing a mission to explaining a decision

Mission P.I.E.D.R.A. brings a navigable base, specialist roles, maintenance activities, historical memories and adaptive feedback into one recurring decision cycle. Its intended contribution is to help young learners make sense of engineering trade-offs through practice and reflection. Each return to the console offers another opportunity to connect evidence with priorities and consequences.

The intended outcome extends beyond the final sol: a learner who can explain what a choice protected, what it cost and why another situation might require a different answer. The browser format and adult-facing report support that conversation in classrooms and at home, while the source records and technical documentation make the project’s foundations available for review.

Enter Mars Base One

The Cloud deployment is the final version of Mission P.I.E.D.R.A. and connects to the project API. GitHub Pages provides a static test version without the backend connection.
